Tiong Bahru's quieter streets tell a story of changing shops, tastes and crowds after hipster heyday
article:
On weekends, Tiong Bahru stirs to life early. Brunch-goers head to cafes like Plain Vanilla , Hello Arigato and Matchaya, while early risers have already picked up their bakes from Tiong Bahru Bakery by mid-morning.

Across the road, the market is busier. Residents and visitors jostle for groceries in the wet market downstairs before heading up for chwee kueh and fried prawn mee, joining queues that can stretch well past the next stall.

All around are the walk-up flats that have long defined Singapore’s oldest public housing estate. Built by the Singapore Improvement Trust in the 1930s, the low-rise blocks have rounded corners and curved balconies, with spiral staircases winding up their backs, in a streamlined Art Deco style rarely seen in public housing since.

The buzz beyond these familiar haunts has softened since Tiong Bahru's heyday as a hipster enclave in the 2010s.

Several independent cafes, bookstores and restaurants that once helped put the neighbourhood on Singapore's lifestyle map have since closed or moved elsewhere.

"The crowds have thinned. Anyone walking Eng Hoon Street on a Saturday can see it," says Bryan Goh, Singapore country manager of sleep and bedding brand Heveya, which has occupied a three-storey conservation shophouse in the estate since 2016.

Despite the quieter streets and departure of some longstanding names, new businesses are still opening in Tiong Bahru, introducing fresh dining and retail concepts.

Healthcare, fitness, beauty and wellness operators have also joined the tenant mix, while established businesses are refreshing their premises.

Property analysts point to a combination of rising operating costs, changing consumer habits, a shrinking residential catchment and greater competition from other lifestyle precincts as possible reasons for the decline in footfall.

Even so, Tiong Bahru's unique heritage and residential character continue to appeal to businesses seeking a foothold in the neighbourhood.

A flourishing enclave and the pressures that followed

Tiong Bahru was built in the 1930s mainly as a residential estate. Its transformation into a lifestyle destination took off in the early 2010s, when independent cafes, boutiques and bookstores started moving in.

“Footfall was limited then, but these businesses could drive their own traffic because people would travel for what they offered,” Ethan Hsu, founder and CEO of retail-focused real estate advisory firm Catbird, tells EdgeProp Singapore .

Relatively low rents allowed businesses to experiment with distinctive, independent concepts that made Tiong Bahru special, adds Hsu, who grew up around the neighbourhood.

As it became more popular, investors bought commercial units to ride the demand from retailers and F&B operators, and rents went up.

“One tenant said back in 2013 that his rent had quadrupled in six years. Those costs were passed on to customers, which weakened demand,” says Hsu.

“Ironically, the enclave’s success in the 2010s led to its decline.”

Real estate consultancy Cushman & Wakefield’s (C&W) analysis of URA Realis data provides some indication of how rents have risen over the past decade.

Average quarterly median ground-floor retail rents in Tiong Bahru’s core heritage and lifestyle precinct increased from $4.62 psf per month in 2016–2019 to $7.02 psf per month in 2023–2026.

These figures — based on properties along Yong Siak Street , Eng Hoon Street, Seng Poh Road, Eng Watt Street and Tiong Poh Road — are indicative given the limited number of transactions and their irregular frequency, C&W notes.

As commercial units in Tiong Bahru are privately held by numerous different owners, there is little visibility into precise rents and occupancy rates.

Catbird’s Hsu notes: “What we can say is that across the wider market, rents are still creeping up while occupied space shrinks. So it is not a collapse of the market, but a symptom of market churn.”

Meanwhile, the Covid-19 pandemic also took a toll on businesses, accelerating changes in consumer habits as more people turned to e-commerce and food delivery.

With lower footfall and higher costs putting a strain on operators, some cafes and shops shuttered or relocated.

Among them were some of the very establishments that had helped make Tiong Bahru the place to be.

Stalwarts depart as newcomers enter the mix

Property investor Peter Chiu has witnessed the turnover of businesses in the estate firsthand.

He bought an apartment in one of the conserved blocks in 2020, rented it out to residential tenants, and has since sold it.

“When I first bought the apartment, Prive Cafe occupied one of the ground-floor units. By the time I sold the apartment, the cafe was gone, and now it’s a new restaurant, Magpie,” Chiu says.

He has seen businesses come and go, including an influx of new dining concepts catering to younger crowds.

“Even a corner bak kut teh shop has become a Toast Box,” Chiu says. “But like most neighbourhoods in rejuvenation, it will go through this period of pain first.”

Several familiar names have left the estate over the years, including Forty Hands, Open Door Policy, PS.Cafe Petit and independent bookstores BooksActually and Woods in the Books.

Hsu observes that the tenant mix now includes more lifestyle services — the likes of healthcare clinics, fitness studios, beauty and wellness operators, art galleries and showrooms.

Some F&B players are also going smaller, with more takeaway counters and grab-and-go formats, and fewer sit-down cafes.

Tiong Bahru's predominantly residential setting presents another challenge for businesses.

With shops and homes sitting close together, many operators must navigate residents' concerns about noise and other disturbances, which can limit activities such as alfresco dining and late-night operations.

“The 2010s were the anomaly, not the baseline,” Hsu says, describing Tiong Bahru's boom at the time as part of a cycle fuelled by novelty, social media and a pioneering group of trendy concepts.

“That cycle has run its course, the same way it did in Holland Village , Chip Bee Gardens and Ann Siang Hill with Club Street.”

Fewer residents and growing competition

Tiong Bahru's retail scene may also be feeling the effects of a shrinking pool of residents living in and around the estate.

Fewer residents in the neighbourhood:

C&W research points to a steady decline during the past decade. The resident population within the Tiong Bahru and Tiong Bahru Station subzones fell about 9%, from about 29,200 in 2016 to 26,400 this year.

The number of residents per dwelling unit also decreased from 2.6 to 2.2 over the same period in those subzones.

“A smaller residential catchment may have moderated growth in neighbourhood-based retail demand,” says Wong Xian Yang, head of research for Singapore and Southeast Asia at C&W.

“While Tiong Bahru has historically drawn visitors from beyond its immediate catchment, a declining resident base may nevertheless have reduced routine and repeat visitation that supports day-to-day retail spending.”

At the same time, visitors have more locations to choose from than a decade ago. These include newer lifestyle clusters such as New Bahru, Joo Chiat and Keong Saik.

Visitor traffic is therefore likely to be distributed across a broader range of precincts today, Wong adds.

A resident identified only as Ng, who has lived in a Tiong Bahru shophouse for about 2.5 years, has noticed the quieter atmosphere, though it is a change he personally welcomes.

He believes some visitors have turned their attention to other up-and-coming lifestyle destinations. “I think people are drawn to the novelty of places like New Bahru,” Ng says.

While New Bahru, located just a short distance away, has probably diverted footfall from Tiong Bahru, Catbird’s Hsu highlights a key difference in how the two precincts operate.

With a concentrated, curated mix of more than 60 brands under one roof and a clear identity, New Bahru has one owner deciding its tenant mix, programming and marketing as a single destination.

“That’s exactly what Tiong Bahru’s fragmented ownership makes so difficult,” Hsu says. “Its trade mix, by comparison, has become diluted, with no critical mass or strong draw to pull people in.”

Fresh experiences in a historic neighbourhood

Amid the changing retail landscape, some businesses continue to find new opportunities in the neighbourhood and build on the heritage, architecture and residential character.

Established businesses are upgrading their premises, while newer arrivals are adding to the estate's dining and retail offerings.

Heveya, for instance, chose to renovate its existing flagship on Eng Hoon Street instead of relocating.

The homegrown bedding retailer’s revamped showroom, unveiled in late October after about three months of renovation, offers a more immersive experience for customers.

“Refreshing the space within the same heritage shophouse felt like a natural next chapter for us, allowing us to build on our roots while showcasing our brand’s evolution over the years,” says Goh.

Heveya’s clientele mainly comprises environmentally conscious buyers in their 40s to 50s who are willing to invest in premium organic sleep products, though Goh has noticed more shoppers in their 30s to 40s keen to experience the showroom.

Where the showroom once existed mainly to let customers try mattresses and learn about natural latex, it now showcases the materials, craftsmanship and philosophy behind the brand alongside the beds.

At the heart of the 2,200 sq ft space is a striking handwoven ramie installation by Bali-based Argentinian artist Clelia. Around it, woven fibre panels, wooden-bead wall art, natural blinds and sculptural bamboo lighting bring texture to the shophouse's heritage architecture.

Curved banquettes and low lounge furniture invite customers to linger, while a tactile display traces latex from tree to mattress.

During EdgeProp Singapore 's visit, the team pointed out the calming earthy palette of what they call “mochaccino walls”.

Customers are encouraged to have a free spinal alignment check before trying the beds. Some come in simply to sleep on the mattresses, occasionally for hours, before deciding on a purchase.

Given the nature of its products, Heveya relies on customers making planned visits rather than passing footfall. “Nobody buys a mattress on impulse between coffees. People come to us deliberately, and many of them live a few doors away,” Goh says.

The showroom also serves a purpose beyond immediate sales, as it helps Heveya build “brand awareness, customer relationships and long-term brand equity”, he adds.

Goh sees value in operating from a heritage shophouse, which he believes offers an experience that conventional retail spaces cannot replicate. “The architectural character and sense of history create a more intimate relationship between the space and its surroundings,” he says.

After nearly a decade in Tiong Bahru, he also considers the estate’s slower pace a good fit for Heveya: “A quiet estate suits a brand built around rest.”

Crafts and curiosities among market stalls

Outside the shophouses, smaller players are finding their way into the estate through humbler, less conventional spaces.

Sideway, a craft and design stall run by photographer-turned-potter Keneth Tan and co-founder Yasha Lai, occupies just 93 sq ft on the first floor of Tiong Bahru Market, among sundry shops lining its outer edge.

Both founders hold weekday jobs and open Sideway mainly on weekends. The market stall offers a smaller-scale setup that suits their part-time operation, without committing to a large retail unit.

For Tan, though, opening in a market was always the intention, as the pair wanted craft to be accessible to everyone.

“As makers ourselves, we believe that craft should exist beyond galleries and exhibition spaces, and instead be more present in everyday life,” he says.

Sideway's shelves hold an ever-changing mix of zines, local ceramics and secondhand objects, including pieces picked up during trips to Japan.

Being in a market also influences their selection, as Tan and Lai lean towards functional pieces such as tableware that people can easily use at home.

Many customers find the stall through social media, which skews the crowd younger, though its location in Tiong Bahru Market also draws people of different ages. Those who stop by include seasoned collectors and people encountering handmade crafts for the first time.

Tan speaks fondly of their neighbouring stallholders, who have been welcoming. Early on, while changing a light bulb, the pair accidentally tripped the main circuit-breaker. The owner of a nearby hardware stall helped them contact the market management to sort it out.

Since then, they have come to recognise familiar faces among their regulars, alongside curious passers-by who wander in to browse or chat.

“That’s the spirit we hope to bring to the neighbourhood: a space where people can slow down amid the hustle and bustle of the market, and perhaps even the fast pace of life in Singapore as a whole,” Tan says.

Bookstore set to move in as bakery gets a makeover

A familiar name in Singapore’s literary circles is preparing to make Tiong Bahru its new home — Book Bar, the homegrown bookstore and cafe founded by Alex Chua and Sara Ng.

Having opened in a Duxton Road shophouse in July 2023, the bookstore will soon relocate to a 2,172 sq ft space at Tiong Bahru Community Centre, roughly twice the size of its existing premises. Renovations are expected to be completed by December.

Chua has spoken about plans to host more book launches, readings and community activities at the larger venue, according to local media reports. Plans include cooking and flower-arrangement workshops, food pop-ups and a wider selection of books.

Book Bar’s arrival in Tiong Bahru bucks a trend. Two other bookstores, once fixtures of Yong Siak Street, have exited in recent years.

Elsewhere in the estate, Tiong Bahru Bakery (TBB), a neighbourhood stalwart since 2012, has given its original outlet on Eng Hoon Street a makeover.

The 60-seat flagship reopened in September 2025 following its first major refurbishment. The redesign includes a self-service island where customers can select their own pastries.

A refreshed visual identity by Singapore branding agency Foreign Policy Design Group features whimsical illustrations and a crescent-shaped logo whose lettering takes a modern spin on the estate's 1930s Streamline Moderne architecture.

“Taking inspiration from Tiong Bahru's architecture gives that identity a connection to where we started, rather than introducing something that could belong anywhere,” says a TBB spokesperson.

“We want returning customers to recognise the bakery they love, while still finding something fresh to enjoy.”

More reasons to linger after dark

Best known for its cafes and bakeries, Tiong Bahru is also gaining a livelier evening crowd at its restaurants.

Magpie debuted on Eng Hoon Street in early 2025, serving what its founders call borderless soul food.

The restaurant is a venture by New Zealand chef-owner Eliot Thomas and Kurt Wagner, founder of Kafe Utu on Jiak Chuan Road and Tamba on Duxton Road.

Magpie’s menu changes regularly, and some ingredients are sourced from Tiong Bahru Market right across the road.

“Tiong Bahru built its name on mornings: bakeries, kopi and brunch. What's changing is that people now want a reason to stay into the evening, and the estate suits that,” says Thomas. “It’s walkable, it has character, and it doesn’t feel like a mall.”

On Tiong Bahru being quieter than before, Thomas admits he never saw it at its busiest, having been in Singapore for only two years.

“I know Tiong Bahru as it is today, and that is the version I chose to open in,” he says.

Dinner trade has been steady, while lunches from Friday to Sunday have also performed well. About half of Magpie's diners live in or near Tiong Bahru, with the rest travelling from across the island.

Families typically dine early in the evening, and groups gather later in the week.

A recently launched cocktail programme gives people a reason to drop by after work or after dinner elsewhere. Taco Tuesdays and skewer nights keep regulars coming back, and collaborations with neighbouring businesses are in the works.

Thomas is also mindful of keeping neighbours onside, given the residential surroundings.

Magpie keeps tables available for residents who walk in, and is careful about noise, deliveries and waste management.

“The aim is for Magpie to feel like it belongs to the estate rather than just being located in it,” he says.

“I’d rather add a steady stream of diners who respect the place than a noisy crowd that wears out the goodwill.”

----------

What could give Tiong Bahru's retail scene a boost?

A precinct-wide, structured placemaking strategy could help reinvigorate Tiong Bahru and attract more visitors, says Wong Xian Yang, head of research for Singapore and Southeast Asia at Cushman & Wakefield.

He suggests an approach similar to the Place Plan developed for the Kampong Gelam historic area.

“Beyond individual events, such an approach would provide a coordinated framework to strengthen Tiong Bahru's identity, curate tenant mix, activate public spaces, and create recurring experiences that encourage visitation,” Wong says.

Ethan Hsu, founder and CEO of Catbird, points out that there remains a catchment, however small, as people still live and work around the estate.

Although Tiong Bahru lacks scale — it does not have enough shops and restaurants to reach the critical mass that pulls crowds to Katong or Kampong Gelam — Hsu thinks that can become an advantage with a clear, well-executed plan to curate the right experiences.

More collaboration among merchants could help put such a plan into action. Businesses may coordinate opening hours, share marketing costs and work out sensible alfresco dining rules with residents.

One approach is to meet the needs of residents and workers nearby, with everyday services, a good neighbourhood cafe and convenience shopping so that they spend locally every day.

Hsu also suggests bringing in destination footfall with concepts that cannot be found anywhere else. Examples are small chef-led restaurants, specialist shops, maker studios running workshops, and galleries open in the evenings.

However, he reckons these ideas will likely only work if rents are affordable and can encourage experimentation.

“Right now, rents do not reward creativity and innovation. Costs are too high, and failure is too expensive, so operators play it safe or do not open at all,” Hsu says.

Daytime activities, including weekend markets and the odd car-free morning, could also encourage visits while minimising late-night noise and disruption to residents.

Tiong Bahru could make more of its heritage story too. “This was Singapore’s first planned housing estate, and walking trails or a small museum in a restored pre-war flat are things that are not easily replicable,” Hsu adds.

Any efforts to increase visitor traffic would have to take into account the estate's predominantly residential setting.

Bryan Goh, Heveya's Singapore country manager, and Eliot Thomas, Magpie's chef-owner, both emphasise that businesses and activities should be mindful of residents and respect their needs.

“In Tiong Bahru, where families live directly above shops, it has to be considerate: daytime, small-scale, and something residents want to join,” Goh says. The kampung spirit, as he puts it, “is built by neighbours who keep showing up for one another”.

For Hsu, the goal is not necessarily to replicate the buzz and crowds of Tiong Bahru's former heyday.

“We are not going to get 2012 back, and we should not try,” he says.

title: WeWork appoints Ryan Jans as Asia Pacific president
article:
WeWork has appointed Ryan Jans as regional president for Asia Pacific (Apac), overseeing its operations across eight countries including Singapore, the flexible workspace provider said in a Nov 20 release. He is based in Sydney.

His priorities include strengthening the performance of WeWork’s existing portfolio, deepening relationships with members and landlords, and delivering a consistent workplace experience across its markets.

“WeWork is in an incredibly strong position in Apac, and there is so much more ground to cover,” Jans said.

Jans previously led WeWork’s revenue teams across Asia Pacific and Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA).

WeWork has 58 locations in Apac, part of a global network of about 600.

WeWork said demand drivers differ across the region. In Singapore, global technology companies, including Chinese businesses setting up regional operations, are driving demand for flexible workspace.

In South Korea, demand is more locally driven, with Korean technology businesses playing an important role.

In Australia, where WeWork marks its tenth anniversary this year, the company sees opportunities in improving occupancy and growing enterprise demand, particularly in Sydney.

John Santora, CEO of WeWork, said Jans’ knowledge of the region and commercial expertise make him well placed to build on the company’s momentum.

title: 3 SGX Blue-Chip REITs Growing Underlying DPU by Up to 11.7%
article:
A bigger distribution feels like good news, but whether it stays that way depends on what funded the increase.
Some increases come from leases that lift rents each year, while others are driven by cheaper loans or a property sale that will not happen twice.
The first kind is more likely to repeat, while the second may fade.
Three SGX-listed
real estate investment trusts (REITs)
have just reported higher distributions per unit (DPU), at least on an underlying basis, and each got there differently.
Here is how to tell which increases are built to last.

Keppel DC REIT’s figures cover nine months, while the other two REITs report full financial years ended 30 September 2026.
Compare the direction of their trends rather than the size of the numbers.
Why is Keppel DC REIT’s DPU growth built into its contracts?
Keppel DC REIT
(SGX: AJBU) owns 27 data centres across 10 countries.
For the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), its DPU rose 11.7% year on year (YoY) to S$0.08571.
Net property income (NPI) grew 13.1% YoY to S$316.8 million, with the REIT crediting positive rental reversions and escalations, as well as the acquisition of Tokyo Data Centre 3.
Escalations are written into contracts, while rental reversions of around 14% for 9M2026 show that tenants accepted higher rents when their leases were renewed.
The REIT sold Kelsterbach Data Centre and lost income from Cardiff Data Centre, while finance costs rose 28.1% YoY.
A larger unit base following the September 2026 private placement also diluted DPU, as the new units were issued before the new assets began contributing rental income.
On 1 October 2026, Keppel DC REIT completed its purchase of an 88.62% effective interest in Tokyo Data Centre 4 and 5.
Both properties are fully occupied, with in-place rents more than 30% below market levels, and management expects the deal to add 2.0% to DPU.
A S$625 million private placement funded part of the purchase, with yen-denominated debt covering the rest.
Aggregate leverage stood at 36.2% as at 30 September 2026 and is expected to rise to 38.8% on a pro forma basis.
Can FCT’s steadier growth continue?
Frasers Centrepoint Trust
(SGX: J69U), or FCT, is Singapore’s largest suburban retail mall owner.
For FY2026, its DPU rose 2.0% YoY to S$0.1235, marking a new high.
The increase was modest, but NPI climbed 15.7% YoY to S$321.7 million, mainly due to a full-year contribution from Northpoint City South Wing.
FCT
also reported higher passing rents across most malls, with retail committed occupancy at 99.7% as at 30 September 2026 and rental reversions of 6.6% for FY2026.
Cheaper borrowing helped too, as FCT’s average cost of debt fell to 3.2% from 3.8% a year earlier.
That benefit, however, depends on interest rates rather than shopper demand.
The acquisition boost is unlikely to repeat, as South Wing is now part of the comparison base.
Distributions from joint ventures also fell 11.7% YoY after a one-off special dividend did not recur.
FCT sold White Sands on 30 September 2026, removing the mall’s income from its portfolio.
Part of the proceeds will be used to repay borrowings and reduce aggregate leverage from 38.7% to 36.8%.
Meanwhile, NEX’s first-phase upgrade is 98% pre-committed and remains on schedule for completion by December 2026.
Why does FLCT’s headline DPU tell the wrong story?
Frasers Logistics & Commercial Trust
(SGX: BUOU), or FLCT, owns 118 logistics, industrial and commercial properties.
For FY2026, total DPU slipped 0.8% YoY to S$0.059.
Strip out distributions from divestment gains, however, and the picture changes, with DPU before these gains rising 9.4% YoY to S$0.057.
Capital distributions from divestment gains fell 71.3%, while higher finance costs also weighed on total distributable income.
The underlying growth has a contracted core, with FLCT pointing to higher annual rental increments from its L&I segment.
L&I occupancy stood at 99.1% as at 30 September 2026.
Across the whole portfolio, leases signed during the year carried rental reversions of 10.4%, while passing rents remained about 9% below market levels.
Other contributors are less dependable, as FLCT benefited from higher average Australian dollar and euro exchange rates, which could reverse.
Finance costs rose 4.6%, while its commercial properties were valued 8.7% below their carrying value and aggregate leverage increased to 39.2%.
Get Smart: Sort the growth before you count it
Behind every
DPU increase
are several sources of growth, and they do not all carry the same weight.
Start with what the leases promise, such as escalations and annual increments.
Then look at what management has achieved through rental reversions and higher occupancy.
Treat cheaper debt and currency gains as bonuses that may not last, and keep one-off distributions on a separate line.
Before celebrating your next DPU increase, ask yourself one question: if interest rates and exchange rates stopped helping, how much of that increase would still be there?

title: Asia finds a surprise currency haven in AI-defying rupee
article:
(Nov 25): The Indian rupee is Asia’s top-performing currency this month, joining a rally in the nation’s equities as investors double down on a hedge against the artificial-intelligence trade.

The currency rallied as much as 0.8% to 92.18 per dollar, its strongest level since March 12. It is also leading emerging-market currencies this quarter, a sharp turnaround after the central bank was forced to announce emergency support measures in early October.

Indian assets have rallied strongly this month even as most Asian stocks and currencies have floundered, as concerns over the AI trade spur a rotation into markets with less exposure to the theme. Overseas funds have poured nearly US$14 billion into local equities in November, after pulling unprecedented sums earlier this year, helping the rupee outperform most global peers.

Lower oil prices are adding to the tailwind by cutting India’s import bill and demand for dollars.

“The recent improvement in INR’s flow backdrop has scope to extend,” said Mitul Kotecha, strategist at Barclays plc. Lower oil prices are cutting India’s demand for dollars to pay for imports while strong foreign equity inflows are adding to the domestic supply of the US currency, he added.

See also: Singapore, China deepen yuan ties with focus on corporates

Barclays has a ‘tactical’ short position on the dollar/rupee, Kotecha said.

title: Russia oil loses price edge in India as Middle East exports rise
article:
(Nov 25): India’s imports of Russian crude are set to decline this month to pre-war levels as a revival of Middle East exports provides buyers with an abundance of cheaper supplies.

Sellers of Russian crude have been slow to cut offer levels to keep up with the falling prices of Persian Gulf oil, according to people familiar with the matter. Iraqi and Saudi Arabian grades have recently been priced at discounts to the Dubai benchmark while Russian Urals remains at a premium, they said, asking not to be named discussing commercial information.

Russia will still remain India’s biggest supplier but its grip on the market has weakened. Imports are poised to average about 1.7 million barrels a day this month, the lowest since February and nearly 40% below July’s record of 2.8 million barrels a day, according to Kpler. Higher freight rates are also eroding the competitiveness of Russian oil given the longer voyage to the subcontinent.

“Shipping from Russia, particularly from the Black Sea, remains expensive due to security risks and logistical uncertainties,” said Sumit Ritolia, senior manager of modelling at Kpler. “Indian refiners are increasingly looking at alternative supplies, not just to optimise crude costs but also to improve supply security and reduce dependence on any single source.”

Indian refiners had been trimming purchases before the Iran war as New Delhi and Washington negotiated a trade deal and the removal of US tariffs. But the conflict in the Middle East disrupted crude supplies to global customers and prompted India to prioritise its energy security.

See also: Europe is beating Asia in fight for gas supply disrupted by war

Overall, India’s crude imports this month are set to shrink to around 4.9 million barrels a day, according to Kpler, the lowest level since August. While Russian purchases are expected to decline, shipments from Iraq and Saudi Arabia are both set to hit the highest since February.

Indian imports of Russian crude are likely to remain near 1.5 million barrels a day in December and into 2027, continuing to rank among the country’s largest suppliers, Ritolia said. But a return to near-record levels seen earlier this year appears unlikely, he said.

title: Europe is beating Asia in fight for gas supply disrupted by war
article:
(Nov 25): Europe’s rush for liquefied natural gas is playing out in the Atlantic Ocean, where high prices are drawing tankers carrying the vital industrial and power-station fuel away from Asia.

Eight vessels with LNG from the US Gulf Coast have changed course to Europe so far this month, according to data intelligence firm Kpler. That is the most since the Middle East war cut off Qatari exports from the global market in late February, making the US the world’s dominant supplier of the super-chilled fuel.

Europe has been aided by relatively weak demand in Asia, allowing it to draw in more gas to limit the drain on inventories that are already at record lows for this time of year. LNG prices in Europe surged to a four-year high last month and that has helped shut the so-called “arb” — the premium that typically lures American gas across the Pacific to China and Japan. Europe is now paying more than Asia since the war began, according to Spark Commodities.

The continent’s success in pulling in cargoes is helping it to meet surging demand for gas as temperatures drop but the high prices that utilities are paying for shipments are already coursing through the economy. Energy-intensive industries like steel, fertilisers and chemicals are faced with steeply higher costs, and some factories are having to suspend operations when power prices get too high while the expensive gas will eventually flow through to household bills and inflation.

“Supply shortages are pulling LNG to the EU, and the profitable trade remains there,” said Carl Larry, an oil and gas analyst at energy consultancy Enverus. “Unfortunately, the EU is paying the premium.”

See also: Japan LNG buying poised to rise as gas power turns profitable

Europe has been able to turn around tankers in the Atlantic thanks in part to the world’s biggest buyers — China and Japan — remaining largely on the sidelines of the spot market. The two countries remain well supplied and have yet to see significant cold snaps that might prompt utilities there to bid for more gas. Northeast Asian inventories are likely sufficient for winter and the current high prices offer little incentive for spot purchases, Rystad Energy said in a note last week.

European imports have jumped more than 45% over the last three months on a 30-day moving average basis while deliveries to Northeast Asia are down about 1%, according to ship-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg. Despite the increase, European Union and UK imports are still slightly lower than last year, an indication the region will need to buy more.

It is the opposite of what happened over the Northern Hemisphere summer when Asian countries — more vulnerable to the energy shock caused by the US-Iran war — competed more aggressively for LNG.

See also: Chinese refiners snapping up cut-price oil to refill stockpiles

That was behind Europe’s struggle to replenish inventories earlier this year so it would have enough over winter, when heating consumption pushes up overall LNG demand. EU storage tanks are now 68% full, compared to a five-year average of 86%, with withdrawals accelerating despite the higher imports.

“Europe has allowed itself to enter winter with extraordinary low stock levels,” said Saul Kavonic, an energy analyst at MST Marquee. “We are going to see increasing direct competition between Northeast Asia and Europe for LNG as winter progresses.”

The need for seaborne gas in Europe is intensifying as the region has been dealing with an early bout of cold, with wrong-footing pundits who had been expecting the El Niño weather pattern to bring milder temperatures. An extended freeze could result in Northwest Europe ending winter with inventories just 14% full, the lowest since 2018, Goldman Sachs Group Inc said in a note this week.

The wide European premium over Asia is likely to continue into the first quarter, especially as the region plans to ban imports of Russian LNG, according to Evan Tan, an LNG analyst at commodities intelligence firm ICIS. “Storage deficit, Russian LNG void and weather-driven demand will likely shut any arb to Asia,” he said.

There is also still a risk that a dip in temperatures in Asia could once again draw LNG away from Europe. Spot electricity prices have surged in Japan this month, making it affordable to import LNG for gas-fired power stations for the first time since February. Already, one Japanese utility has bought an LNG shipment for December delivery while selling a cargo for March, according to traders.

For now, outlooks for China, Japan and South Korea are pointing to milder-than-normal temperatures — at least in the short term. That could allow Europe to keep soaking up US LNG without a deeper price war with Asia, although predicting the weather remains a fickle business.

“Asia is only one cold spell or pickup in utility demand away from bidding it back in their favour," said Toby Copson, China-based managing partner at Davenport Energy, which trades oil and gas. “If that happens, we’ll see competition for spot cargoes pick up rapidly.”

title: Metals rout deepens as AI, Fed worries fuel bearish sentiment
article:
(Nov 25): Copper, aluminium and tin all added to Tuesday’s fierce selloff in metals as tech stocks extended losses and traders braced for US inflation data that will feed the Federal Reserve’s next moves on interest rates.

After muted early trading, prices on the London Metal Exchange moved decisively lower, with copper adding to a slump of more than 5% on Tuesday to near its lowest level this year. Aluminium fell as much as 0.9% and tin fell nearly 4%.

Metals have tumbled this month — despite some near-term supply tightness — in a rout fuelled by doubts over the artificial intelligence boom, as well as the prospect of Fed hikes and possible trade action by the Trump administration. There are also mounting worries over softer consumption in China.

“The price declines reflect concerns about downward revisions to AI-related capital spending,” said Li Xuezhi, head of research at brokerage Chaos Ternary Futures Co. “Combined with weak domestic demand in China, this is also likely to lead to lower estimates for global aggregate demand.”

Copper, in particular, has been swept up in the bearish turn for AI stocks, after optimism about demand from data centres helped carry the metal to a record near US$15,000 a tonne in September. Technology shares have extended declines this week after a brief bounce on Monday that followed Jensen Huang’s unexpected return to head chipmaker Nvidia Corp following a scandal.

Three-month copper fell 0.7% to US$11,738 a tonne on the LME by 3.05pm in Singapore while aluminium dropped 0.8% to US$2,747 a tonne. Tin, which shed 7.3% on Tuesday, dropped 3.8% to US$38,020 a tonne.

See also: LME to list major new aluminium brand as historic squeeze deepens

Metals are falling even as buyers scramble to get hold of prompt supplies, signalled by steep backwardations on futures markets and rising physical premiums. Nearby spreads on aluminium narrowed significantly later on Tuesday after the LME unleashed rule changes to cope with an intensifying squeeze on nearby positions.

The LME’s main mechanism to address squeezes — known as its ‘Tom-next lending rules’ — now applies to those with positions equal to more than 30% of available aluminium stockpiles, down from 50%. The exchange also tightened lending requirements for traders holding major positions for longer than five days.

Aluminium's key cash-to-three-month spread fell to US$67.53 a tonne on Tuesday, from more than US$400 on Monday.

See also: China extends pause on US minerals ban to maintain truce

Investors will be watching the Fed’s preferred gauge of inflation, personal consumption expenditure, which is due later Wednesday (Nov 25). Investors have already fully priced in a quarter-point rate increase next month. The Trump administration could also announce plans for new tariffs on China and other major economies, which has the potential to spook the market.

“The fact that prices continued to slump despite the absence of any new negative catalysts suggests that the selloff was driven more by sentiment than fundamentals,” said Michael Wu, base metals derivatives trader at Jiangsu Xinbu New Materials Technology Group. “We probably shouldn’t be this pessimistic.”

title: Maybank reviews portfolio as chip curbs hit data centres
article:
(Nov 25): Malaysia’s largest bank is reviewing its portfolio for potential exposure to the latest US chip curbs, as it assesses how the restrictions could affect data centre clients and their funding needs.

“There is an increased level of scrutiny that is obviously required, given the new developments and the new policies affecting the compute financing,” Michael Oh-Lau, chief executive officer of Maybank Investment Bank Bhd, said in an interview with Bloomberg TV’s Haslinda Amin.

Maybank will get clarity from its clients to ensure “they’re still well positioned to proceed with the financing requirements that they have”, he said.

Lenders are launching sweeping reviews of data centre projects in the wake of tougher rules to curb Chinese companies’ use of advanced US chips in Southeast Asian nations. Banks from Citigroup Inc to Standard Chartered plc are pressing clients for further details on who uses their chips and seeking proof they’re in line with stricter export-control rules enacted by the US Commerce Department, Bloomberg reported Wednesday.

Though there’s little public data, analysts estimate anywhere from 30%-45% of Malaysia’s data centre capacity is linked to Chinese demand. While data centres also serve local and Western clients, the fastest-growing and more lucrative segment has been Chinese firms needing overseas access to advanced chips for artificial intelligence (AI) training.

Estimates by Natixis SA show that Southeast Asian banks are the second largest source of funding for China-linked data centres, after Chinese lenders. Banks in the region, especially Singapore and Malaysia, will likely take a hit from the latest chip curbs, Natixis said in a report on Monday.

See also: Banks put data centre clients under microscope on AI chips — Bloomberg

“Investors will need to recalibrate and adjust to the new norm,” Oh-Lau said. Still, he expects strong investment momentum to continue into 2027.

Malaysia’s economy has expanded above expectations for much of the year, supported by resilient domestic spending and demand linked to AI, which has fuelled semiconductor exports and a surge in data-centre investment. Officials are assessing the potential impact of new US restrictions on growth, though the central bank governor predicted that the tech upcycle will be sustained into next year.

Oh-Lau sees a strong pipeline of initial public offerings for 2027 following a blowout year for new share sales this year as more local companies reach scale. He expects some standout listings in the healthcare and technology sectors.

See also: Trump threatens to tax firms building data centres abroad

While geopolitical shocks and sharp movements in rates and currencies may affect sentiment, Oh-Lau said investors are beginning to see Malaysia as a defensive market against risk.

“We’ve never been this busy,” Oh-Lau said of 2026, adding that “Malaysia is a good place to be.”

title: German economic growth revised down as investment sinks
article:
(Nov 25): Germany’s economy expanded at a slower pace than first thought in the third quarter as investment slumped.

Gross domestic product rose 0.1% between July and September, less than the 0.2% preliminary reading, the statistics office said Wednesday (Nov 25). While government spending jumped 0.3% from the previous three months and private consumption increased 0.1%, capital investment sank 1.2%.

The economy is still on track for its best year since 2022 after German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government launched a vast public-spending drive to shore up infrastructure and defence capabilities.

Exports, the country’s traditional growth driver, also played a key role in the first half of the year as companies benefited from the global investment boom in artificial intelligence. The pharmaceutical industry probably saw extra demand before new US tariffs and chemical firms got a temporary boost from the Iran war hurting Asian competitors.

That changed in the third quarter as goods exports fell 0.8%, driven by decreases in cars, chemicals and metals, Destatis said. Imports dropped even more strongly, however.

See also: Eurozone activity holds steady as Germany offsets French slump

Michael Herzum, an economist at Union Investment, said private investment remains the weak point of Germany’s recovery.

“The high level of geopolitical uncertainty during the summer months dampened companies’ willingness to invest,” he said in a statement, adding it’s crucial that firms resume doing so to expand production.

Commerzbank chief economist Joerg Kraemer said the development shows companies’ disappointment about the government’s inability to enact economic reforms.

See also: French companies to announce €14.9 bil in investments

The Bundesbank has said activity will pick up again in the final quarter as exports regain momentum. Overall, the government’s economic advisers expect 1.3% expansion in GDP this year followed by 1% in 2027.

title: UK energy bills rise 26% as war fuels cost-of-living squeeze
article:
(Nov 25): UK households are set for a sharp rise in energy costs in January as the Middle East war pushes up wholesale gas and electricity prices, with winter demand adding further pressure.

Ofgem’s price cap, which limits how much suppliers can charge consumers per unit of energy, will rise 26% to £2,166 (US$2,833) from Jan 1, the watchdog said in a statement on Wednesday. This is the steepest rise since October 2022, at the height of Europe’s energy crisis following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

The increase adds to the cost-of-living squeeze as the war in Iran pushes up inflation and borrowing costs across the economy. It also threatens to erode government efforts to ease pressure on households, while strained public finances leave ministers with limited room to cushion the blow.

“For too long, British families have been paying the price for conflicts overseas and volatile fossil fuel markets,” Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said in a statement.

The price households will pay for each unit of gas they use jumped 38% from the previous cap to a record, surpassing even the level seen at the height of the last energy crisis.

See also: YTL PowerSeraya targets more commercial customers while maintaining leading position in residential market

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has sought to shield homes by cutting VAT on energy costs, while ministers added further support in the October Budget, including a £100 payment for millions of households. This latest increase risks swallowing up much of that relief.

Bills are expected to remain above £2,000 throughout 2027, according to forecasts from energy consultancy Cornwall Insight Ltd, with prices forecast to fall just 1% when the cap changes again in April. Wholesale energy prices have surged since the US-Iran war began earlier this year, with UK gas futures and power contracts more than doubling.

“We would love to be able to point to a moment when the outlook will turn around, but the honest answer is that it depends on what happens in the Middle East,” said Craig Lowrey, retail markets principal at Cornwall Insight.

See also: Coal miners need their rivals to go bust

The surge in energy prices has already pushed inflation to 3.6%, the highest level in a year. Officials raised interest rates in November for the first time in more than three years to prevent price pressures from spreading across the economy, and markets expect another hike at the December meeting.

The price rise will start to feed through to the broader economy next year. The cap is fixed for three months, locking in higher energy costs through the winter and contributing to Bloomberg Economics’ expectation that inflation will accelerate further.

Higher prices for longer will deepen the strain on vulnerable homes that has persisted since the 2022 energy shock. Many households are already struggling to pay their bills, and domestic energy debt reached a record £5 billion in the second quarter, almost double its level three years earlier.

title: Indra raises revenue guidance to more than €12 bil by 2030
article:
(Nov 25): Spanish defence and technology company Indra Sistemas SA raised its guidance on Wednesday (Nov 25) as new chairman Ángel Simón unveiled his strategy after a management shake-up earlier this year.

Indra said it now expects revenue of more than €12 billion by 2030 and a slightly higher margin than before. The company previously targeted €10 billion in 2030, though management said in February that it expected to reach that level sooner.

The Madrid-based company also raised its 2026 revenue guidance to €7 billion from €6 billion.

The investor day is the first under Simón and chief executive Josep María Recasens, who took up their roles this year after a reorganisation at the top of the partly state-owned group.

Simón replaced Ángel Escribano in April after weeks of tensions over the company’s direction and pressure from the government, which wields influence over Indra through state holding company Sepi, its largest shareholder. The strategy is being presented just days before Spain’s Nov 29 general election.

Indra has been one of the beneficiaries of a sharp increase in Spanish and European military spending, with the company’s defence revenue doubling in the first nine months of 2026 and its overall order backlog up 133% year-on-year as of September.

See also: Asia data centre sound out US clients to replace China demand

The new strategy also comes as Spain’s anti-corruption prosecutor investigates allegations of irregularities in the award of some government defence contracts involving Indra and Escribano Mechanical & Engineering, the company controlled by Ángel Escribano and his brother Javier.

title: China, US set for ‘new chapter’ of trade talks, ex-official says
article:
(Nov 25): China and the US will make more headway once their trade talks resume in January, when their year-old tariff truce is set to expire, according to a former top Chinese economic official.

“They will open a new chapter and make trade relations between China and the US more healthy,” Zhu Guangyao, who was China’s vice minister of finance from 2010 to 2018, said in an interview with Bloomberg TV in Singapore on Wednesday. While “some differences” may remain, he said the negotiators will “continue to talk and make that progress step by step.”

His upbeat comments follow days after President Donald Trump’s visit to Shenzhen for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping during a gathering of Asia Pacific economies. Both Xi and Trump appeared to lean heavily on their personal rapport to keep ties between their countries on an even keel, even as fresh strains have emerged between the world’s biggest economies, including an alleged spy scandal involving involving Nvidia Corp chief executive officer Jensen Huang.

Zhu served as deputy finance minister until his retirement in 2018, overseeing the Customs Tariff Department and playing a key role in US-China trade negotiations.

As soon as on Tuesday, the US is set to announce plans to raise tariffs on goods from countries including China, as the Trump administration moves to replace levies struck down by the Supreme Court.

The duties are expected to target economies accused of hurting American industry by subsidizing their domestic manufacturers, Bloomberg News has reported. The tariffs on Chinese products are expected to be broader in nature than charges on items from others and will lack exemptions, though they will be within the bounds of the trade ceasefire President Xi Jinping reached with his US counterpart, Donald Trump, last year in South Korea.

See also: Starbucks said to engage banks for sale of Japan business — Bloomberg

Zhu said that issues arising from Washington’s investigation into excess manufacturing capacity under Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act can be settled through negotiations.

title: IOI Properties defends Malaysian REIT IPO pricing as parent trades 40% below book, sees room for upside
article:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 25): IOI Properties Group Bhd (KL:IOIPG) on Wednesday defended the pricing of the initial public offering (IPO) of its real estate investment trust (REIT), saying the listing let the developer monetise its assets at book value while its own shares trade at about a 40% discount.

IOI Properties group chief executive officer and IOIPG Malaysia REIT (KL:IOIREIT) executive chairman Datuk Lee Yeow Seng said the final IPO price of 91 sen per unit matches the trust’s pro forma net asset value (NAV) per unit.

He added that the group had also chosen to leave room for potential upside for investors instead of maximising the IPO price.

“Currently, IOI Properties is actually priced at about 40% below book value, so we actually are able to create value by listing IOIPG Malaysia REIT at book value,” he told reporters at a press conference following the REIT’s listing ceremony on Wednesday.

“We don’t want to price the IPO to the maximum, where there’s no upside and nothing left on the table for the investors,” he added.

IOIPG Malaysia REIT’s final IPO price was set at 91 sen per unit, 5.2% below the initial indicative retail price of 96 sen.

See also: IOIPG Malaysia REIT opens lower in trading debut

The Malaysian public portion of the IPO, the largest-ever REIT listing in Malaysia, was oversubscribed by just 0.59 times.

Maybank Investment Bank Bhd regional head of equity capital markets Raymond Chooi, meanwhile, clarified that the indicative retail price of 96 sen stated in the prospectus was the top of the pricing range, and that the final offer price was determined through the bookbuilding exercise.

“It was never set at 96 sen to begin with. It is a maximum price because in a bookbuilding process, there is never certainty. And that (process) also provides us some flexibility in terms of pricing the REIT,” he said.

See also: DayOne said to pause US IPO plans on data center, market concerns — Bloomberg

Chooi said the final price of 91 sen took into account prevailing market sentiment and feedback from investors, while ensuring that the valuation was acceptable to the issuer.

Maybank Investment Bank and AmInvestment Bank Bhd are the joint principal advisers and joint global coordinators for the IPO.

IPO proceeds to fund debt repayment, capex and acquisitions at sponsor level

The IPO, which was structured entirely as an offer for sale of existing units, raised about RM2 billion ($626.7 million) for IOI Properties, with no fresh capital raised by the REIT itself.

Meanwhile, IOI Properties shareholders were entitled to purchase one REIT unit for every 10 existing IOIPG ordinary shares held.

When asked about the decision against issuing new units to raise funds for the REIT, IOIPG Malaysia REIT head of finance Alvin Loo said IOI Properties had already earmarked the proceeds from the listing exercise for its own funding requirements, including debt repayment, capital expenditure and acquisitions.

“For us, we have already earmarked the proceeds from this REIT exercise to repay some of our borrowing, and also this will be utilised for the capital expenditure that we already anticipated, including some of the acquisitions that we have at the sponsor level,” he said.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

IOIPG Malaysia REIT has an initial portfolio of nine properties valued at RM7.66 billion, comprising IOI City Mall in Putrajaya, six hotels operating under Marriott International’s brands and two office developments

Separately, Lee said IOI Properties is working on a proposal for its board’s approval for a secondary listing on the Singapore Exchange (SGX), which the property developer is targeting to undertake in 2027.

“We are targeting around next year. If anything, we need to table it to the board first for approval,” he said.

“Currently, the management is working on the groundwork to prepare a proposal to be brought forward to the board.”

IOI Properties had previously disclosed that it had begun engaging the SGX over a potential secondary listing.

The property developer has a sizeable presence in Singapore, with assets including IOI Central Boulevard Towers in the city-state’s central business district and the South Beach integrated development.

At the time of writing, shares in IOI Properties were trading down one sen or 0.34% at RM2.90, valuing the property developer at RM17.56 billion. Meanwhile, IOIPG Malaysia REIT was trading down three sen or 3.3% at 88 sen, with a market capitalisation of RM4.84 billion.

title: IOIPG Malaysia REIT opens lower in trading debut
article:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 25): IOIPG Malaysia Real Estate Investment Trust (KL:IOIREIT) slipped in its Main Market trading debut on Wednesday amid a broader market decline.

The trust opened at 87 sen versus its initial public offering (IPO) price of 91 sen per share. IOIPG Malaysia fell to as low as 86.5 sen and paused for noon trading break at 87.5 sen after more than 19 million shares changed hands.

Market capitalisation stood at RM4.8 billion ($1.5 billion) based on the last price.

“We are not in a short-term business,” IOIPG Malaysia executive chairman Datuk Lee Yeow Seng said at a post-listing news conference. “We are here for the long run. What we want to try to achieve is to create value for our stakeholders, including our investors, our tenants, as well as our partners.”

The decline comes even after IOIPG Malaysia cut the final price by five sen in Malaysia’s largest-ever REIT IPO following lukewarm investor reception. A portion of the IPO was undersubscribed and had to be allocated to other categories of investors. Overall, demand from the average retail investors came in only slightly above the available shares.

The trust will also have to brave prospects of rising interest rates and other market uncertainties.

See also: DayOne said to pause US IPO plans on data center, market concerns — Bloomberg

IOIPG Malaysia has an initial portfolio of nine properties valued at RM7.66 billion, anchored by IOI City Mall in Putrajaya, alongside six hotels operating under Marriott International’s brands and two office developments.

The last REIT to be listed was Paradigm Real Estate Investment Trust (KL:PARADIGM), which opened flat in June 2025. Big Caring Group Bhd (KL:BCG), the most recent entrant to the Main Market, also opened below its IPO price in its trading debut.

On Wednesday, Kenanga Investment Bank initiated coverage on IOIPG Malaysia with ‘outperform’ call and target price of RM1.20, joining Affin Hwang Investment Bank that rated the trust a ‘buy’ with target price of RM1.12 ahead of the listing.

See also: The biggest winners in Anthropic’s landmark IPO

At its opening price of 87 sen, the implied distribution yield rises to 7.28% from 6.96% based on its IPO price. The trust has a distribution policy of paying at least 90% of its distributable income to unitholders on a quarterly basis.

The spin-off listing forms part of the efforts by sponsor IOI Properties Group Bhd (KL:IOIPG) to pare down its borrowings and strengthen its balance sheet. The property developer also previously said it was exploring a separate trust for its Singapore assets.

The IPO raised about RM2 billion entirely for IOI Properties, with no fresh capital raised by the trust itself.

Maybank Investment Bank Bhd and AmInvestment Bank Bhd are the joint principal advisers, joint global coordinators, joint bookrunners, joint managing underwriters and joint underwriters for the IPO.

DBS Bank Ltd is a joint global coordinator and joint bookrunner.

CIMB Investment Bank Bhd, Hong Leong Investment Bank Bhd, RHB Investment Bank Bhd and UOB Kay Hian (M) Sdn Bhd are the joint bookrunners and joint underwriters. Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Ltd is also a joint bookrunner.

title: Asia data centre sound out US clients to replace China demand
article:
(Nov 25): Data centres across Asia are racing to offload excess computing power to US buyers after the Trump administration tightened a loophole that gave Chinese tech firms access to Nvidia Corp’s most advanced chips.

That’s according to Ronit Jain, chief executive and co-founder of Liquid Compute, a New York-based startup building a regulated exchange for AI computing capacity. A new rule targeting exports of cutting-edge AI accelerators to the region is hitting data centre providers that were counting on renting computational resources to Chinese customers, he said.

The cost to access Nvidia’s powerful B300 graphics processing units was US$7.72 per GPU-hour at the end of last month, according to a Liquid Compute index. That had fallen 7% to US$7.19 as of Tuesday, according to the startup, which says it tracks over 200 data centre companies. A post Jain made on X last week highlighting the declining prices drew widespread attention.

“All the neoclouds based in Asia-Pacific selling to Tencent and other companies, or in Singapore or Taiwan with Chinese companies as offtakers, have excess capacity,” Jain said in an interview. “They’re trying to broker it into the US.” He declined to name the companies selling their excess compute, or the buyers.

I would expect B300 pricing to continue declining.

A staggering number of neoclouds have approached us @liquidcompute looking to remarket long-term B300 capacity originally committed to Chinese-affiliated offtakers into the US and Western Europe due to concerns of stricter… — Ronit Jain (@ronitrjain) November 19, 2026

This time last year, the price of B300s stood at US$4.55 per GPU-hour and had steadily increased before falling over the course of the last month, Jain said.

See also: Huawei found guilty of US criminal charges in landmark case

Nvidia’s board reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as chief executive officer this week, 11 days after he resigned amid revelations that he’d had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman the US government has investigated for spying on behalf of China. At the heart of the scandal was the woman’s company, Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which was alleged to have been smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China.

The US government last week said shipments of advanced chips to four countries in Southeast Asia will require Washington’s permission. It also announced a soon-to-come global clampdown on data centres that provide Chinese firms with remote access to advanced hardware they’re restricted from buying.

New York-based Liquid Compute, which was founded in 2024, tracks over 200 neoclouds, many of them with operations in Asia-Pacific, Jain said. In September, the startup raised US$15 million in a seed round co-led by FirstMark Capital and Chemistry Ventures. The company is also backed by startup accelerator Y Combinator.

See also: Ex-RBI chief Rajan sees Nvidia governance risk with return of Huang

Before the controversy, Nvidia’s Huang had been among the most vocal advocates of Chinese chip buying. Even with his reinstatement, market participants appear to be operating under the assumption that Chinese firms will no longer be able to access Nvidia’s chips via AI cloud providers, according to Jain.

“Just based on basic economics, you would expect the price to decrease with a temporary influx of supply,” he said.

title: Bitcoin funds head for worst month as outflows near US$5 bil
article:
(Nov 25): US-listed exchange-traded funds investing in bitcoin are heading for the worst month of outflows since their 2024 debut, as a persistent selloff in the world’s largest cryptocurrency drives investors away.

A net US$4.71 billion has been withdrawn from the funds in November so far, according to data compiled by Bloomberg through Nov 23. BlackRock Inc.’s iShares Bitcoin Trust, the largest fund holding the token, has suffered about US$4 billion of redemptions this month, also putting it on course for its worst monthly outflow.

The exodus comes as bitcoin tumbles below US$60,000 and heads for its worst monthly performance since June 2022, when a string of corporate failures triggered a broader crypto-market meltdown. The token has dropped about 23% this month and was trading around US$59,200 as of 1pm Wednesday in Singapore, down about 1% in the Asia session.

The losses underscore a sharp reversal for a group of ETFs that helped propel bitcoin higher after their US debut in January 2024. The funds opened the cryptocurrency to a wider pool of institutional and retail investors and became an important source of demand during the bull market. Their record redemptions are now reinforcing the current downturn as that source of buying dries up.

Bitcoin briefly recovered alongside other risk assets on Monday after Nvidia Corp reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, but has since surrendered all of those gains, a sign that investors are using rallies to reduce exposure.

See also: Bitcoin fails to hold Nvidia bump with crypto headwinds in focus

“When a market cannot hold a rally on good news, it usually means that investors are using any strength to sell,” data analytics firm Glassnode said in a note. “Bitcoin trades around the clock and tends to be one of the first assets sold when investors want less risk.”

Bitcoin is facing numerous headwinds at the moment, from high-profile hacks that have undermined confidence in its security to the prospect of higher interest rates and greater regulatory scrutiny following recent US midterm elections. The absence of US demand is adding to the pressure, according to Glassnode.

See also: Bitcoin ETF exodus gathers pace, removing key source of support

“The ETFs and other institutions were an important source of demand on the way up, and there is little interest from them at these prices,” the firm said. “A return to ETF inflows, together with net buying on Coinbase, would be the first sign that this is changing.”

Bitcoin is also facing greater competition for investor capital as money gravitates toward equities and assets offering income, according to Ayesha Kiani, chief operating officer of Monarq Asset Management.

Bitcoin is “competing for the same risk capital that is going into equities right now,” Kiani told Bloomberg Television, describing the ETF exodus as “concerning.”

The cryptocurrency industry may need a fresh catalyst to revive demand after the forces that drove the previous rally have faded, she said.

“I think we do need to find a new narrative, a new catalyst, a new market, something new for the entire industry for us to become that emerging asset class again,” Kiani said. “There are better yield-bearing assets out there at this point. So, like, why bitcoin?”

title: Malaysia’s EPF to boost overseas stakes, likes infrastructure
article:
(Nov 25): Malaysia’s largest pension fund aims to increase its overseas investments to 50% in five to six years as it repositions its RM1.5 trillion (US$365 billion) portfolio in an environment of higher stock valuations and bond yields and heightened geopolitical uncertainty, its chief executive officer said.

“That’s where I see the portfolio going,” Employee Provident Fund CEO Ahmad Zulqarnain Onn said in an interview with Bloomberg Television’s Haslinda Amin on Wednesday. Currently, the state-run mandatory retirement savings fund for private sector workers has 38% of its total portfolio invested overseas.

The fund favours investing in infrastructure, Ahmad said, adding that trends around AI, digitisation and energy transition are driving a lot of infrastructure spending.

One of Asia’s largest retirement funds, EPF manages RM1.5 trillion in assets for its more than 16 million members. In the last ten years, EPF has paid an average annual dividend of about 5.9%, more than double the 2.7% earnings from Malaysian banks’ one-year fixed deposits over the same period.

title: Starbucks said to engage banks for sale of Japan business — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 25): Starbucks Corp has tapped advisers to prepare for a potential sale of its Japan business for several billion dollars, according to people familiar with the matter.

The US coffee chain is working with banks including Citigroup Inc and Morgan Stanley and has started sounding out interest from some strategic and financial investors, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information isn’t public. A formal process might start as soon as this year, they said.

Starbucks has about 2,000 coffeehouses in Japan, making it one of the company’s biggest markets. Deliberations about the business are ongoing and might not result in a sale, the people said.

A Starbucks spokesperson said the company continually assesses the best structure for its customers and creating value for shareholders. The chain has a strong business in Japan, where it’s been for more than 30 years, the spokesperson said.

Bloomberg News reported in June that Starbucks was considering options for the Japanese business and had held preliminary talks with banks.

See also: AI chip boom to see won build on best year in almost a decade

Starbucks doesn’t break out standalone revenue for Japan, but combined with Canada and the UK, the three accounted for about 72% of net revenues generated outside the US and China in fiscal 2026.

title: 新项目推出转移买家视线 10月私宅转售量减少5.9%
